posts.query: Do mineral sunscreens reflect UV light?
posts.card_title: Mineral sunscreen does not work by reflection
posts.capsule: Mostly not. Measured across the UV range, reflection and scattering account for only about 4–5% of what zinc oxide and titanium dioxide do — less than SPF 2. The rest is absorption, the same mechanism chemical filters use (Cole et al., 2016). That study measured specific formulations in vitro, so treat the figure as the shape of the answer, not a constant.
facts: Reflection accounts for roughly 4–5% of UV attenuation
Absorption does the rest — as in chemical filters
Cole et al., 2016 · in vitro, specific formulations

posts.query: Is natural skincare safer than synthetic skincare?
posts.card_title: Natural is not a safety category
posts.capsule: It is not a claim about safety. Natural describes where an ingredient came from, not how the skin responds to it — plant extracts are among the more common contact allergens, and many well-tolerated ingredients are synthesised. What matters is the concentration, the formulation, and whether your barrier can currently tolerate it.
facts: Origin is not a measure of tolerance
Botanical extracts are common contact allergens
Concentration and formulation decide the outcome

posts.query: Can I tell if a skincare product will suit me from the ingredient list?
posts.card_title: An ingredient list is not complete information
posts.capsule: Only partly. The list gives you order and identity, not concentration, not pH, not the delivery system, and not how the ingredients behave together. Two products with near-identical lists can feel entirely different on the same face. It is a useful filter for known triggers and a poor predictor of everything else.
facts: No concentrations, no pH, no delivery system
Near-identical lists can behave differently
Useful for avoiding known triggers

posts.query: How many steps should a Korean skincare routine have?
posts.capsule: Fewer than you have been told. Reducing the number of products is more reliably protective than upgrading them, because every additional step is another chance to irritate a barrier that is already working. The ten-step routine is a retail format, not a clinical one. Most guests leave here using less than they arrived with.
facts: Each added step is another chance to irritate
Reduction is more reliable than substitution
The ten-step routine is a retail format

posts.query: Why does my new skincare product sting?
posts.card_title: If it stings, that is information
posts.capsule: Stinging usually means the barrier is compromised rather than that the product is working. A barrier holding water in and irritants out does not register most well-formulated products at all. If something stings on you, the useful next step is repair, not persistence — and we would rather tell you that than let you conclude skincare is not for you.
facts: Stinging signals barrier compromise, not efficacy
Repair first — actives afterwards
Persisting through it usually costs you time

posts.query: Should I use retinol or acids while travelling?
posts.card_title: Actives on a trip — probably not
posts.capsule: Usually not, and not because they are bad. Travel already loads the barrier with cabin air, a different climate, sun and disrupted sleep. Introducing a new active into that is how a good product gets blamed for a bad week. Repair first. The actives will still be there when you are home and stable.
facts: Travel already loads the barrier
A new active in a bad week reads as a bad product
Repair before actives, always

posts.query: What does skin barrier mean and why do Korean estheticians talk about it?
posts.capsule: Your barrier is the outermost layer that holds water in and keeps irritants out. When it is compromised, skin flushes, stings, and absorbs product without improving — which is why upgrading products rarely fixes it. Everything we do is ordered around that layer, and nothing active goes on top of a barrier that cannot hold it.
facts: Holds water in, keeps irritants out
A compromised barrier makes good products fail
Repair precedes actives, without exception
